title: Top Talkers in an Access Log
statement:
Write `top_ips.sh [-n N] [-s STATUS]`. It reads a web server access log on **stdin** and prints the IP addresses that made the most requests.

Each line looks like:
```
203.0.113.5 - - [10/Oct/2026:13:55:36 +0000] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 2326
```
(the IP is the 1st field, the HTTP status the 9th).

- Print `COUNT IP` lines: the top `N` (default 3), most requests first, ties by IP.
- `-s STATUS` counts only requests with that status (e.g. `-s 404`).
- `-n` must be a positive integer; otherwise, or for an unknown option, print a message to stderr and exit 2.
- Empty input prints nothing and exits 0.
harness:
log() { printf '%s - - [10/Oct/2026:13:55:36 +0000] "GET %s HTTP/1.1" %s 512\n' "$1" "${3:-/}" "$2"; }
sample() {
  log 10.0.0.1 200; log 10.0.0.2 200; log 10.0.0.1 404; log 10.0.0.3 200
  log 10.0.0.1 200; log 10.0.0.2 404; log 10.0.0.4 500; log 10.0.0.2 200
  log 10.0.0.10 200; log 10.0.0.10 404
}
(
  cd "$(fresh_dir)"; sample > access.log
  run_solution < access.log
  expect_eq "top 3 by default, ties by IP" $'3 10.0.0.1\n3 10.0.0.2\n2 10.0.0.10' "$out"
)
(
  cd "$(fresh_dir)"; sample > access.log
  run_solution -n 1 < access.log
  expect_eq "-n limits the output" "3 10.0.0.1" "$out"
)
(
  cd "$(fresh_dir)"; sample > access.log
  run_solution -s 404 < access.log
  expect_eq "-s filters by status" $'1 10.0.0.1\n1 10.0.0.10\n1 10.0.0.2' "$out"
)
(
  cd "$(fresh_dir)"; sample > access.log
  run_solution -n 10 -s 500 < access.log
  expect_eq "fewer results than N" "1 10.0.0.4" "$out"
)
(
  cd "$(fresh_dir)"
  run_solution < /dev/null
  if [[ $status == 0 && -z $out ]]; then pass "empty input: no output, exit 0"
  else fail "empty input: no output, exit 0" "status=$status stdout=[$out]"; fi
)
(
  cd "$(fresh_dir)"
  ok=1
  for bad in 0 -3 abc 2x; do
    run_solution -n "$bad" < /dev/null
    [[ $status == 2 && -n $err ]] || { ok=0; detail="-n $bad gave status=$status stderr=[$err]"; }
  done
  run_solution -x < /dev/null
  [[ $status == 2 ]] || { ok=0; detail="-x gave status=$status"; }
  if (( ok )); then pass "bad -n values and unknown options exit 2"; else fail "bad -n values and unknown options exit 2" "$detail"; fi
)
reference_solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# top_ips.sh [-n N] [-s STATUS] < access.log
usage() {
  echo "usage: top_ips.sh [-n N] [-s STATUS] < access.log" >&2
  exit 2
}

n=3
status=""
while getopts ":n:s:" opt; do   # leading ':' = we handle errors ourselves
  case $opt in
    n) n=$OPTARG ;;
    s) status=$OPTARG ;;
    *) usage ;;
  esac
done

if ! [[ $n =~ ^[1-9][0-9]*$ ]]; then
  echo "top_ips.sh: -n must be a positive integer" >&2
  exit 2
fi

awk -v want="$status" 'NF >= 9 && (want == "" || $9 == want) { print $1 }' |
  sort | uniq -c |
  awk '{ print $1, $2 }' |      # normalise uniq's padded output to "COUNT IP"
  sort -k1,1nr -k2,2 |          # count descending (numeric), then IP
  head -n "$n"
hints: `while getopts ":n:s:" opt; do case $opt in ...; esac; done` parses the options; `$OPTARG` holds each option's value.
`sort -r` sorts *text*, so `10` comes before `9`. Use `sort -k1,1nr -k2,2`: numeric reverse on the count, then the IP as a tie-breaker.
`awk -v want="$status" '$9 == want'` filters by a field; pass shell values in with `-v` rather than splicing them into the program text.
discussion:
This is the bread and butter of on-call work: `sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head` answers "who is hammering us?" in seconds.

Where the quick version goes wrong:
- **`sort -r` is a text sort.** "10" sorts before "9", and the starter happily reports the wrong top talker. `-n` makes it numeric; `-k1,1nr -k2,2` adds a deterministic tie-break, which matters for reproducible output (and for tests).
- **`cut -d' '` is fragile** with variable spacing; `awk` splits on runs of whitespace.
- **`getopts`** handles `-n 5`, `-n5` and grouped flags correctly, and the leading `:` in the option string lets you print your own message and choose the exit code.
- **Validate numeric arguments.** `head -n abc` fails with a confusing error, and `head -n 0` silently prints nothing.
- **Never splice user input into an `awk` program** (`awk "\$9 == $status"`). That's code injection. Pass it with `-v`.

**Follow-ups:** How would you handle a 50 GB log faster? (One `awk` pass with an associative array instead of sorting everything.) How would you do this for a live log? (`tail -F` plus a periodic summary.)
